teile.einleitung: Cumulating (in German “kumulieren”) is a word from electoral law and means writing a name twice on the ballot paper. This gives your favourite candidate two votes at once. In Switzerland this is allowed in many elections, for example in the National Council elections.
wichtigste: Cumulating means writing a name twice on the ballot paper.
The cumulated person thus receives two votes instead of just one.
In the National Council elections you may write a name at most twice.
Cumulating is only common in proportional elections with lists.
Parties sometimes put names on their list twice already; this is called pre-cumulating.
The word comes from the Latin “cumulare”, which means to pile up.
Together with splitting your vote between lists (panachage), cumulating gives voters a lot of freedom.

abschnitte.text: When **cumulating**, you write the name of a person twice on the ballot paper. This shows that you would particularly like to see this person in parliament. He or she then receives two **candidate votes** from this voter. In the end, who is elected depends on who has the most votes within their list.

In the **National Council elections** a name may appear on the ballot paper at most twice. If someone writes a name down three times, the third entry is struck out. In total you may only write down as many names as the canton has seats. The canton of Zurich, for example, has had exactly 36 seats since the 2023 election, so its ballot paper has 36 lines.

Some parties print the names of their candidates on the list twice already. This is called **pre-cumulating**. That way these people automatically receive double votes if someone hands in the list unchanged. Parties often do this when they only have a few candidates, so that the list is still full.

Cumulating goes together with **panachage**. With panachage you write names from other lists on your ballot paper. You can also cross out names you do not want to vote for. These options only exist in **proportional elections**, in which seats are distributed according to the strength of the parties.

Through cumulating, voters can decide for themselves which people from a party are elected. So they do not just vote for a party but also for very specific people. This gives citizens more influence. In some other countries this is not possible; there the party alone decides the order of its list.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sheet on which you write the names in an election.
A person who stands for election.
A ballot paper with the names of a party's candidates.
An election in which seats are distributed according to the parties' share of the vote.

gewusst: In some German federal states you may also cumulate in local elections, there sometimes even up to three votes per person.
Anyone who writes a name three times on the ballot paper does not make it invalid; the third entry simply does not count.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. That is why the country also has four names: Schweiz, Suisse, Svizzera and Svizra.
wichtigste: The four national languages are German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Around 6 in 10 people have German as their main language.
Switzerland is called Suisse, Svizzera and Svizra.
The French-speaking part is called Romandy.
In German-speaking Switzerland people speak Swiss German in everyday life.
“Allegra” is a Romansh greeting.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Constitution** names four **national languages**: German, French, Italian and Romansh. German is the most common: around **6 in 10** people in Switzerland have German as their main language. It is followed by French, Italian and Romansh, which only a small minority speaks. Many people also speak other languages, for example English, Portuguese or Albanian.

**German-speaking Switzerland** lies in the north, east and centre of the country. The French-speaking west is called **Romandy** or Western Switzerland. Italian is spoken mainly in **Ticino** and in some valleys of the Grisons. **Romansh** is spoken in parts of the **Grisons**, for example in the Engadine. Some cantons such as Fribourg, Valais and Bern are bilingual, and the Grisons is even trilingual.

In everyday life, people in German-speaking Switzerland mostly speak **dialect**, that is **Swiss German**. There are many different dialects, for example Bernese German or Basel German. At school people write **High German**, also called Standard German. Newspapers and books are also mostly written in Standard German.

In French Switzerland is called **Suisse**, in Italian **Svizzera** and in Romansh **Svizra**. In Italian you say hello with **“Buongiorno”** and goodbye with **“Arrivederci”**. In French you say “Bonjour” and “Au revoir”. A typical Romansh greeting is **“Allegra”**, which you hear in the Engadine, for example.

gewusst: Coins and stamps often say “Helvetia”, the Latin name of Switzerland, so that no national language is favoured.
Romansh has been a national language of Switzerland since a popular vote in 1938.

teile.einleitung: When you draw lots, chance decides. For example, you pull a slip of paper out of a hat or toss a coin. This is fair because everyone has the same chance.
wichtigste: When drawing lots, chance decides.
You can draw lots with a coin or with slips of paper in a hat.
Pulling out a slip without looking is called drawing lots.
When drawing lots, everyone has the same chance.
In a tie, lots can decide.
In National Council elections, too, lots can decide when the votes are equal.

abschnitte.text: When you **draw lots**, **chance** decides what counts. For example, you write two names on slips of paper and put them in a hat. A child pulls out a slip **without looking**. This is called **drawing lots**. The name on the slip that is drawn wins. Nobody can know beforehand what the result will be.

A **coin** can also be used to draw lots. A coin has **two sides**: heads and tails. That is why it is a good choice when you have to choose between two suggestions. Before the toss you agree which side stands for which suggestion. Then you toss the coin and see which side lands face up. In football, for example, this is how the choice of ends is decided before the match.

When drawing lots, **each side has the same chance**. Nobody is favoured, and nobody can influence the result. That is why lots are often used when there is a **tie**. If, for example, two candidates have the same number of votes, lots can decide. That way there is still a result and everyone can accept it.

Drawing lots also exists in politics. If two people have exactly the same number of votes in the **National Council elections** but there is only one seat, **lots** decide. This is laid down in the **Federal Act on Political Rights**. It happens very rarely. But in **2011** in **Ticino**, lots really did have to decide between two people.

gewusst: In ancient Athens many offices were not elected but allocated among the citizens by lot.
The word “lottery” is related to the word lot.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland most judges belong to a party. Many regularly pay their party part of their income. This levy is called a mandate tax or mandate levy.
wichtigste: With the mandate levy, judges give part of their income to their party.
The parties describe the contributions as voluntary, but in practice they are expected.
The party nominates candidates, who therefore do not have to run their own election campaign.
GRECO of the Council of Europe criticises the mandate levy.
Critics see the independence of the judiciary at risk.
For the year 2023 the Swiss Federal Audit Office published the contributions of federal judges for the first time.

abschnitte.text: The judges of the **Federal Supreme Court** are elected by the **Federal Assembly**. In practice the **parties** nominate the candidates. The seats are distributed roughly according to the strength of the parties. This has an advantage for the candidates: they do not have to run **their own election campaign**, because the party secures them the necessary votes in parliament. In return the party expects regular money from the elected judges.

The **mandate levy** is not a state tax. It is a payment that elected office-holders make to their own party. There is **no legal obligation** to pay it. The parties therefore stress that the contributions are **voluntary**. In fact, however, elected judges are expected to pay. According to SRF, in 2020 judges from the Greens paid around **15,000 francs** a year, and those from the SP about 13,000 francs. For many parties this is an important **source of income**.

**GRECO**, the Group of States against Corruption of the **Council of Europe**, criticises the close ties between judges and parties. It calls for federal judges to stop paying a mandate levy. Critics fear that judges remain financially and politically **dependent** on their party. But judges should only be bound by the **law**. The mandate levy could thus weaken the **independence of the judiciary**. Internationally, this practice is very unusual.

For a long time it was unclear exactly how much money was involved. Under the new **transparency rules** on political financing, parties must report contributions from office-holders every year. The **Swiss Federal Audit Office** published the contributions of federal judges for the year **2023** for the first time. So today anyone can look up how much the judges pay their parties. Supporters of the current system say that party membership makes the political views of judges openly visible.

gewusst: In 2021 the voters clearly rejected the Justice Initiative. It wanted federal judges to be chosen by lot from a pool of experts.
Many cantonal judges and other elected office-holders also pay their party a mandate levy.

teile.einleitung: The large dome is the landmark of the Federal Palace in Bern. On the outside it is green; on the inside a coloured glass dome shines with the Swiss coat of arms and the coats of arms of all the cantons.
wichtigste: The outside of the dome is covered with copper.
The green colour comes from the patina on the copper.
Inside there is a dome made of coloured glass.
In the middle is the Swiss coat of arms, around it are the cantonal coats of arms.
The dome bears the words “Unus pro omnibus, omnes pro uno”.
The coat of arms of the canton of Jura was only added in 1981.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Palace** in Bern is the seat of parliament and government. The outside of its dome is covered with **copper sheeting**. Copper reacts with air and rain and over time forms a turquoise-green layer. This layer is called **patina**. It forms by itself and protects the metal.

Beneath the outer dome is an **inner dome made of coloured glass**. This lets light into the **Dome Hall**. In the middle you can see the **Swiss coat of arms** as a mosaic, surrounded by oak leaves and held by two female figures. All around it the **coats of arms of the cantons** are painted on glass. They stand for the cantons that together form Switzerland.

The dome bears the Latin motto **“Unus pro omnibus, omnes pro uno”**. This means **“One for all, all for one”**. The motto expresses that the cantons stick together. It is regarded as the unofficial motto of Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: The coat of arms of Jura
abschnitte.text: When the Federal Palace was built, the **canton of Jura** did not yet exist. It was only created in 1979 as the youngest canton of Switzerland. Its coat of arms was added to the glass dome in **1981**. Since then all the cantons have been represented in the dome.

There are several figures in the Dome Hall. By the stairs of the entrance hall stand **two bears**; the bear is the heraldic animal of Bern. On the staircase in the Dome Hall there are four bronze figures of **mercenary soldiers (Landsknechte)**. Each one stands for one of the **four national languages** of Switzerland.

gewusst: The Federal Palace was opened in 1902; the architect was Hans Wilhelm Auer.
You can visit the Federal Palace on free guided tours.

teile.einleitung: Legislative planning is the Federal Council's roadmap for four years. It sets out which goals the government wants to achieve in a legislative period and how it intends to pay for them.
wichtigste: A legislative period at federal level lasts four years.
At the start of each legislative period the Federal Council presents parliament with its dispatch on legislative planning.
The 2023 to 2027 legislative planning has four guidelines and 25 goals.
One guideline concerns protecting the climate and natural resources.
The annual goals make the planning concrete for each year.
In its management report the Federal Council shows what it has achieved.
The legislative financial plan adds the financial side to the planning.

abschnitte.text: A **legislative period** is the term of office of parliament and government. At federal level it lasts **four years**. After the elections the National Council is completely re-elected, and the Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council anew. At the start of each legislative period the **Federal Council** writes a **dispatch on legislative planning**. In it, it sets out its political guidelines and goals for the next four years.

The goals are arranged under **guidelines**. A guideline is a big topic under which there are several goals. In the **2023 to 2027** legislative planning there are **four guidelines** and **25 goals**. One guideline concerns, for example, prosperity and digitalisation, another the **protection of the climate and natural resources**. Each goal comes with concrete **measures**. In the 2019 to 2023 legislative period there were still three guidelines.

The Federal Council proposes the legislative planning, but **parliament** debates it. The National Council and the Council of States can change goals, delete them or add new ones. At the end they adopt the plan. In this way government and parliament decide together where politics should go in the coming years.

Good plans need money. That is why legislative planning includes a **legislative financial plan**. It shows how the planned projects are to be financed. So that the planning is not just on paper, the Federal Council sets **annual goals** every year. They are derived from the legislative planning and describe the steps for a single year.

abschnitte.titel: Accounting for it in the management report
abschnitte.text: At the end of each year the Federal Council takes stock. In the **management report** it compares its goals with the results. The report goes to parliament. There it is examined by the **Control Committees**. They check whether the government and the administration have done good work. This makes visible what has been achieved and what has not.

gewusst: Legislative planning is a cycle: plan, carry out and then account for it in the management report.
Many cantons and municipalities also draw up their own government programme for their term of office.

teile.einleitung: The rule of applicable law (in German “Massgeblichkeitsgebot”) is an important rule of the Federal Constitution. It is in Article 190 and says that the courts must apply federal laws and international law, even if a federal law contradicts the constitution.
wichtigste: The rule of applicable law is set out in Article 190 of the Federal Constitution.
The article bears the heading “Applicable law”.
Federal laws and international law are binding on the Federal Supreme Court and all authorities that apply the law.
Even a federal law that contradicts the constitution must be applied.
The Federal Supreme Court can, however, examine cantonal laws for their constitutionality.
The court may find that the constitution has been breached, but must still apply the law.

abschnitte.text: Article 190 of the **Federal Constitution** bears the heading **“Applicable law”**. It says, in essence: **federal laws** and **international law** are binding on the Federal Supreme Court and the other authorities that apply the law. Binding means that they must apply these rules. This rule is called the **rule of applicable law** or **duty to apply**. It applies not only to the Federal Supreme Court but also to administrative authorities and cantonal courts.

In many countries a constitutional court can strike down a law if it breaches the constitution. In Switzerland this is not possible for **federal laws**. There is no **constitutional review** of federal laws here. Even an **unconstitutional** federal law remains applicable. One reason for this: federal laws are passed by parliament, and the people can vote on them with a **referendum**. That is why they should have the last word, not the judges.

Article 190 is a **duty to apply**, not a **ban on examination**. So the Federal Supreme Court may investigate whether a federal law is compatible with the constitution. It can also **find** that there is a breach. But it must still apply the law. With such a finding, however, the court can prompt the legislator to correct the law.

Article 190 only protects federal laws and international law. With **cantonal laws** it is different. The Federal Supreme Court can examine whether a cantonal act is compatible with the Federal Constitution. If it breaches it, the court can **strike it down** or **not apply** it in an individual case. In this way the Federal Supreme Court ensures that the cantons respect fundamental rights and federal law.

It becomes difficult when a federal law and an international treaty contradict each other. In the **Schubert** case in **1973**, the Federal Supreme Court decided that the legislator can **deliberately** depart from older international law. Then the more recent federal law takes precedence. This is called the **Schubert practice**. The Federal Supreme Court later restricted this practice where **human rights** are concerned.

gewusst: In Switzerland, for federal laws, it is not a court but ultimately parliament and the people who have the last word.
There have been several attempts in parliament to introduce constitutional review for federal laws, but they were rejected.

teile.einleitung: After its meetings, the Federal Council informs the public at a press conference. There members of the Federal Council and the Federal Council spokesperson explain what the government has decided.
wichtigste: The Federal Council usually meets once a week.
The press conferences usually take place in the Federal Palace Media Centre in Bern.
They are led by the Federal Council spokesperson, who is also Vice-Chancellor.
The responsible members of the Federal Council present their items of business.
Under the principle of collegiality, they also defend decisions they themselves opposed.
Press releases are also published.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Council** normally meets **once a week** in the Federal Palace in Bern for its meeting. There it makes many decisions. Afterwards the most important of them are announced publicly. This is what the **press conference** is for. It usually takes place in the **Federal Palace Media Centre** and is also broadcast on the internet. So anyone can watch.

The responsible members of the Federal Council present their items of business themselves and answer questions from journalists. The conference is led by the **Federal Council spokesperson**. He is also **Vice-Chancellor** in the Federal Chancellery. He also gives information about other decisions. Besides the conference, the Federal Council publishes its important decisions on the day of the meeting as **press releases**. So everyone can find out directly.

The Federal Council decides as a **collegial body**, that is as a group of seven members with equal rights. Under the **principle of collegiality**, all of them defend the decisions together in public. This also applies when a member was outvoted internally. That is why a federal councillor sometimes presents a decision at the press conference that he or she personally opposed. Differing opinions usually remain **confidential**.

gewusst: You can follow the Federal Council's press conferences live on the internet.
The Federal Council consists of seven members, all with equal rights.

teile.einleitung: With a constructive vote of no confidence, the German Bundestag can remove the Federal Chancellor. But at the same time it must elect a successor, so that the country is never without a government.
wichtigste: The constructive vote of no confidence is set out in Article 67 of the Basic Law.
The Bundestag must elect a new chancellor with a majority of its members.
There must be 48 hours between the motion and the vote.
Up to 2025 there were two such votes in the Bundestag, in 1972 and 1982.
The rule is a lesson learned from the Weimar Republic.
Spain also has the constructive vote of no confidence.

abschnitte.titel: The rule in the Basic Law
abschnitte.text: According to **Article 67 of the Basic Law**, the Bundestag can only express its lack of confidence in the Federal Chancellor by **electing a successor**. It then asks the Federal President to dismiss the previous chancellor. What is needed is the **chancellor majority**, that is a majority of all the legal members. Abstentions and absences therefore count like no votes. There must be **48 hours** between the motion and the vote.

In the **Weimar Republic** from 1919 to 1933, opposing parties could join forces to bring down a government. Afterwards they often failed to form a new majority. Governments were therefore very **unstable**. This was not to happen again. That is why the Basic Law requires a new majority to choose a new chancellor straight away.

In **1972** Rainer Barzel (CDU) tried to replace Federal Chancellor **Willy Brandt**. He missed the required majority by two votes. Later a member of parliament admitted to having received money for abstaining. In **1982** the second attempt succeeded: Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as Federal Chancellor. Up to 2025 there were only these two votes.

With the **destructive** or simple vote of no confidence, a majority against the government is enough. Whether a new majority then comes about remains open. **Spain** also has the constructive form, the “moción de censura”. In June 2018 the Spanish parliament used it to replace Mariano Rajoy with **Pedro Sánchez**. In **Switzerland** there is no vote of no confidence: the Federal Council is elected for four years and cannot be removed by parliament.

gewusst: Helmut Kohl is so far the only German Federal Chancellor who came into office through a constructive vote of no confidence.
The word “constructive” means “building up”: you do not just bring a government down, you build a new one at the same time.

teile.einleitung: When many people have to decide something together, they vote. The winner is then usually the majority, that is the side with more votes. This is how decisions are made in the class, in the municipality and in the whole of Switzerland.
wichtigste: In a vote, the side with more votes wins.
The majority is the larger group.
The smaller group is called the minority.
More than half of the votes is always a majority.
The result of a vote applies to everyone.
The minority deserves respect too.
In a democracy, the majority decides.

abschnitte.text: The word **majority** comes from the Latin for “greater”. It is the group that has **more votes** than the other. An example: 12 children want to play football, 8 children want to play dodgeball. 12 is more than 8. So football has the majority and is played. The group with fewer votes is called the **minority**.

Sometimes a proposal needs **more than half** of all the votes. In a class of 20 children, half is 10. So more than half means **11 votes** or more. This is called an **absolute majority**. If there are several proposals, often the one with the **most votes** simply wins. With 7 votes for painting, 9 for singing and 4 for crafts, singing wins. This is called a **relative majority**.

After a vote, the **result applies to everyone**. Even those who lost take part. This is sometimes not easy, but it is part of democracy. Next time you can vote again, and perhaps your own idea will win then. The majority must never **make fun of** the minority. The children who lost deserve **respect** too, and their opinion is just as important.

In a **democracy** people have a say. What the majority wants is done. In Switzerland the people vote several times a year. Some votes even need two majorities: the majority of voters, the **majority of the people**, and the majority of the cantons, the **majority of the cantons**. In this way both the many people in large cantons and the small cantons count.

gewusst: Changes to the Federal Constitution in Switzerland always need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
Sometimes votes are very close, and then only a few votes decide.

teile.einleitung: A lampion is a colourful paper lantern with a light shining inside it. In Switzerland lanterns belong to 1 August, the national holiday, when children walk through the village in the evening carrying glowing lanterns.
wichtigste: A lampion is a lantern made of paper.
Inside, a candle or a small lamp shines.
A small battery lamp is safer than a candle.
On 1 August there are lantern processions in many places.
Many 1 August lanterns show the Swiss cross.
You carry the lantern on a stick.

abschnitte.text: A **lampion** is a colourful **paper lantern**. The paper is stretched over a frame, often in the shape of a ball or a cylinder. Inside, a light shines. In the **dark** the coloured paper glows especially beautifully. Paper lanterns have also been known in China and Japan for a long time.

In the past people put a **candle** in the lantern. But a candle can set the thin paper alight. That is why today people often use a **small battery lamp**. It has no flame and is therefore safer. You carry the lantern on a **stick**, so it stays well away from your body.

On **1 August** Switzerland celebrates its **national holiday**. In the evening, children in many villages and towns walk in a **lantern procession**. Many lanterns bear the **Swiss cross** or a **cantonal coat of arms**. Afterwards there is often a bonfire on a hill, a speech and music. Because the processions take place in the evening, you can see the lights well.

gewusst: 1 August commemorates the Federal Charter of 1291, which is regarded as the founding document of the Swiss Confederation.
Only since 1994 has 1 August been a public holiday throughout Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Magna Carta is a famous charter from England. In 1215 King John (John Lackland) had to use it to recognise the rights of his subjects. It is regarded as an early step towards the rule of law.
wichtigste: King John sealed Magna Carta in 1215.
“Magna Carta” means “Great Charter”.
It was sealed in the meadow of Runnymede on the Thames.
The barons forced the king to do so.
The charter is written in Latin.
No free man could be imprisoned without a lawful judgement.
Four original copies from 1215 survive.

abschnitte.text: **King John**, known as John Lackland, was King of England in the early 13th century. He demanded high taxes and lost expensive wars. The **barons**, the powerful nobles, were very angry about this. They rebelled against the king and wanted to limit his power. In **1215** they forced him to recognise their demands in a charter.

The Latin name **“Magna Carta”** means **Great Charter**. “Magna” means great, “Carta” means charter or document. In German it is also called the Great Letter of Freedom. The charter was written in **Latin**, like most important documents in Europe at the time. It was sealed in the meadow of **Runnymede** on the **Thames**, west of London. That is where King John and his opponents met.

The originally continuous text was later divided into **63 clauses**. Many of them deal with dues and the rights of the barons. The most famous is one principle: no **free man** may be imprisoned or punished except by a **lawful judgement** or according to the law. This means: even the king is not above the law. This idea shapes the **rule of law** to this day.

At first Magna Carta did not last long. **Pope Innocent III** took King John's side. In August 1215 he declared the charter **null and void**, that is invalid. Later, however, it was **reissued** in a changed form. In this way its idea stayed alive and was confirmed again and again in England.

**Four original copies** of the 1215 Magna Carta still survive. Two are in the **British Library** in London, and one each in the cathedrals of **Lincoln** and **Salisbury**. Most of the clauses were repealed in the 19th and 20th centuries. In the United Kingdom only **three clauses** still apply today, including those on the freedoms of the Church and the rights of the City of London.

gewusst: Magna Carta is over 800 years old and is still quoted today as a symbol of freedom and justice.
King John was the younger brother of the famous King Richard the Lionheart.

teile.einleitung: Every year the Corruption Perceptions Index compares how strongly corruption in politics and administration is perceived in different countries. It is published by the organisation Transparency International.
wichtigste: The index is published by Transparency International.
Transparency International was founded in Berlin in 1993.
Its founder was the former World Bank manager Peter Eigen.
The index has existed since 1995.
Since 2012 the scale has run from 0 (very corrupt) to 100 (very clean).
In the 2025 index Denmark was in first place.

abschnitte.text: **Corruption** means that someone misuses their power to gain advantages for themselves. One example is **bribery**: someone pays an official so that he or she grants a permit. Corruption is hard to measure directly because it usually happens in secret. That is why the index measures **perceived** corruption in the **public sector**.

The organisation **Transparency International** was founded in **Berlin** in **1993**. Its founder was the German **Peter Eigen**. As a director of the World Bank in Africa, he had experienced the consequences of corruption. Today the organisation has national chapters in over 100 countries, including **Switzerland**. It has published the index since **1995**, usually at the end of January or the beginning of February.

The index brings together assessments by **experts** and **businesses**. From these, each country receives a score. Since 2012 the scale has run from **0** for very corrupt to **100** for very clean. The higher the score, the less corruption is perceived. No country has yet reached 100 points. The 2025 index covers 182 countries and territories.

In the 2025 index, published in February 2026, **Denmark** was in first place, just ahead of Finland. **Switzerland** also regularly ranks among the ten best countries. At the bottom there are often countries with war and weak institutions. In the 2024 index **South Sudan** was in last place.

gewusst: The worldwide average in the 2025 index was only 42 out of 100 points.
The Nordic countries such as Denmark, Finland and Norway have been among the top group of the index for many years.

teile.einleitung: Congress is the parliament of the United States of America. It consists of two chambers, the Senate and the House of Representatives, and meets in the Capitol in Washington.
wichtigste: Congress consists of the Senate and the House of Representatives.
The Senate has 100 members, two from each state.
The House of Representatives has 435 voting members.
Senators are elected for six years, representatives for two years.
Congress meets in the Capitol in Washington.
With two thirds in both chambers it can override a veto by the President.

abschnitte.text: **Congress** consists of the **Senate** and the **House of Representatives**. Both chambers must approve a law. They meet in the **Capitol**, a building with a large dome on Capitol Hill in Washington. This is similar to Switzerland, where the National Council and the Council of States together form the Federal Assembly.

The Senate has **100 members**. Each of the 50 states sends **two senators**, no matter how big it is. This is reminiscent of the **Council of States**, where most cantons have two seats. Senators are elected for **six years**, and every two years about a third are newly chosen. The Senate must approve international **treaties** with a two-thirds majority.

Since 1913 the House of Representatives has in principle had **435 voting** members. The seats are distributed among the states according to **population**, as with the National Council. The whole House is re-elected **every two years**. It is led by the **Speaker of the House**, who is elected by the representatives. The Speaker is second in line to succeed the President, after the Vice President.

The President can stop a law with a **veto**. However, if **two thirds** in both chambers vote for it, the law comes into force anyway. The **Vice President** officially presides over the Senate. In the event of a tie, he or she casts the **deciding vote**. In this way parliament and government check each other; this is called the **separation of powers**.

gewusst: As Vice President from 2021 to 2025, Kamala Harris cast more deciding votes in the Senate than anyone before her.
Besides the 435 voting members, the House of Representatives also has delegates, for example from the capital Washington, who are not allowed to vote.

teile.einleitung: The Landsgemeinde is the assembly of all the voters of the canton of Glarus. Once a year they meet in the open air in the cantonal capital Glarus and decide on laws, taxes and elections by raising their hands.
wichtigste: The Glarus Landsgemeinde takes place on the Zaunplatz in Glarus.
It is usually held on the first Sunday in May.
In the canton of Glarus you may vote from the age of 16.
In 2007 Glarus was the first canton with a voting age of 16.
You can only be elected to a cantonal office from the age of 18.
Before the Landsgemeinde every household receives the Memorial with all the items of business.
The government has five members and is elected at the ballot box.

abschnitte.text: The **Landsgemeinde** is a very old form of direct democracy. Instead of putting papers into a ballot box, the voters gather on the **Zaunplatz** in the middle of Glarus. They stand in a large circle, the so-called ring. Today there is a Landsgemeinde in only two cantons: Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden. Many visitors from all over Switzerland come to watch every year.

Anyone who wants to vote holds up their **voting card**. This shows that the person is allowed to vote. The Landammann presides over the assembly and estimates with the naked eye which side has more hands. If it is very close, he or she has the vote held a second time. Another special feature is that everyone may speak and put forward **motions**. So a proposal can be changed directly at the assembly.

So that everyone is well prepared, the canton sends out the **Memorial** beforehand. This booklet goes to every household with voters. It contains all the items to be voted on, with explanations. This allows the people of Glarus to form an opinion at home. At the Landsgemeinde itself, they then discuss and decide.

On **6 May 2007** the Landsgemeinde decided to lower the voting age for the canton to **16**. Glarus was thus the first canton in Switzerland to take this step. Since then young people have been able to have a say on cantonal and municipal questions. However, you can only be elected from the age of 18. This is called the **right to stand for election**. In federal votes the age of 18 still applies.

The Glarus government, the **Regierungsrat**, has **five members**. They are not elected at the Landsgemeinde but **at the ballot box**. The Landsgemeinde then decides which of them becomes **Landammann**. The Landammann chairs the government and presides over the Landsgemeinde. There is also the cantonal parliament, the Landrat, which prepares the items of business.

gewusst: In 2006 the Landsgemeinde decided to merge the canton's 25 municipalities at the time into just three large municipalities.
Because motions can be put forward at the Landsgemeinde, a proposal is sometimes passed in a completely different form from the one the government proposed.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland a concordat is a treaty between two or more cantons. The cantons use it to carry out shared tasks, for example in schools, prisons or grants for students.
wichtigste: A concordat is a treaty between cantons.
According to Article 48 of the Federal Constitution it must not run counter to the Confederation.
Each canton decides for itself whether to join.
The hooligan concordat is aimed at violence at sports events.
The cantons work together in three prison concordats.
The school concordat of 1970 coordinated the schools for the first time.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **cantons** have many tasks of their own. Some tasks are easier to solve together. For this, cantons conclude **concordats**, that is treaties with each other. According to **Article 48 of the Federal Constitution**, such treaties must not run counter to the law and interests of the Confederation. The rights of other cantons must also be respected.

Each canton decides according to its **own law** whether to join a concordat. Often the **cantonal parliament** approves it, sometimes the people do so in a **vote**. No canton can be forced to join. That is why not all cantons always take part in a concordat.

With the **school concordat** of 1970, the cantons agreed, for example, on the age at which children start school and the length of compulsory schooling. It was later developed further by **HarmoS**. The **grants concordat** sets minimum standards for education grants. The **Intercantonal University Agreement** states that the canton of residence pays a contribution when someone studies in another canton.

The so-called **hooligan concordat** is really called the Concordat on Measures against Violence at Sports Events. It makes possible, for example, **area bans**, that is bans on being near a stadium. For prisons there are three **prison concordats**: North-western and Central Switzerland, Eastern Switzerland, and Latin Switzerland. In them the cantons run institutions together.

gewusst: The word “concordat” also refers to treaties between a state and the Holy See, that is the Catholic Church.
A concordat can be very small: sometimes only two neighbouring cantons conclude a treaty, for example for a shared school.

teile.einleitung: Value added tax is a tax you pay when shopping. It is included in the price of almost all goods and services. For the Confederation it is one of the most important sources of income.
wichtigste: Switzerland has had value added tax since 1 January 1995.
It replaced the old turnover tax on goods, WUST for short.
In the end consumers bear the tax.
Within the country it is collected by the Federal Tax Administration, on imports by Customs.
Thanks to the input tax deduction, only the added value is taxed.
A special rate of 3.8 per cent applies to hotel stays (as of 2025).
Since 2024 the tax has been slightly higher to finance the AHV.

abschnitte.text: **Value added tax (VAT)** is included in the price of almost everything you buy. Businesses pay the tax to the Confederation. But they add it to the price. So in the end it is paid by **consumers**, that is everyone who buys something. On many till receipts you can see how much VAT is included in the price.

A loaf of bread is made in several stages: the farmer supplies grain, the mill makes flour, the bakery bakes the bread. At each stage some value is added, an **added value**. A business may deduct the VAT it has itself paid to suppliers from its own tax bill. This is called the **input tax deduction**. In this way, at each stage only the newly created added value is taxed.

Value added tax was introduced on **1 January 1995**. Switzerland introduced it later than most European countries. Before that the Confederation levied the **turnover tax on goods**, **WUST** for short. It taxed mainly goods but hardly any services. With the **AHV 21** reform, the people and the cantons accepted an increase in VAT in 2022. Since **2024** the additional money has gone to the **AHV** old-age insurance.

There is not just one tax rate. Since 2024 the **standard rate** has been 8.1 per cent. For everyday necessities such as food, books and medicines a **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent applies. For **hotel stays** there is a **special rate** of 3.8 per cent (as of 2025). It is meant to support **tourism** in Switzerland.

Within the country the **Federal Tax Administration (FTA)** is responsible for VAT. It also checks businesses' tax returns. For goods **imported** into Switzerland, the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** collects the tax at the border. In this way imported goods are taxed in the same way as goods from within the country. Anyone with a turnover of less than **100,000 francs** a year does not have to account for VAT. Small businesses can, however, register voluntarily.

gewusst: Value added tax is one of the Confederation's largest sources of income.
Even if you shop online abroad, you often pay VAT when the goods are imported into Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In a constitutional monarchy there is a king, a queen, a prince or an emperor as head of state. However, their power is limited by a constitution, and the country is usually governed by an elected government.
wichtigste: “Constitution” means the basic law of a state.
In a constitutional monarchy the monarch is bound by the constitution.
Examples are the United Kingdom, Spain and Japan.
Switzerland's neighbour Liechtenstein is a principality.
In a parliamentary monarchy the monarch has mainly ceremonial duties.
In an absolute monarchy, by contrast, the ruler has unlimited power.

abschnitte.text: The word **“constitution”** means the basic law of a state, its **charter**. In a constitutional monarchy even the **monarch** must keep to the constitution. The office is usually inherited within a family. The opposite is an **absolute monarchy**: there the ruler is not bound by any constitution. A well-known example of this is **Louis XIV** of France.

In many monarchies today the **elected government** makes the political decisions. This is then called a **parliamentary monarchy**. The monarch has mainly **ceremonial duties**: receiving guests, opening parliament and representing the country. In Great Britain the King reads out the **“King's Speech”** at the opening of Parliament. The text, however, is written by the government.

Since September 2022 the head of state of the **United Kingdom** has been **King Charles III**. He is also head of state of other countries such as Canada and Australia. **Spain**, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Sweden are also monarchies. In **Japan** an **emperor**, the Tenno, is head of state; he has only symbolic duties. Germany, Italy and Portugal, on the other hand, are republics.

Switzerland's neighbour **Liechtenstein** is a **principality**. The head of state is a prince. Its constitution combines the monarchy with **democratic rights** of the people, for example popular votes. The prince has more influence there than the monarchs in most other European countries. **Switzerland** itself is a republic without a monarch.

gewusst: Charles III became king when his mother Elizabeth II died in September 2022. She had been queen for around 70 years.
Liechtenstein uses the Swiss franc as its currency.

teile.einleitung: A majority election (in German “Majorzwahl”) is an electoral system in which the people with the most votes are elected. That is why it is also called a majoritarian election. In Switzerland, the Council of States is elected this way in most cantons.
wichtigste: In a majority election, whoever gets the most votes wins.
Another name for it is majoritarian election.
The Council of States is elected by majority vote in almost all cantons.
In the first round you usually need an absolute majority, that is more than half the votes.
In the second round a relative majority is enough, that is simply the most votes.
The cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel elect their members of the Council of States by proportional representation.
Most cantonal governments are also elected by majority vote.

abschnitte.text: In a **majority election** the focus is on people, not parties. Whoever gets the most votes is elected. The other candidates get nothing, even if they had many votes. The word comes from the Latin “maior”, which means greater.

In the first round you usually need an **absolute majority**. This means you must get more than half of the valid votes. If nobody manages this, there is a **second round**. There a relative majority is enough, so whoever simply has the most votes is elected.

The **Council of States** has 46 seats; each canton sends two people, and the six former half-cantons one each. The cantons decide for themselves how they elect their members of the Council of States. Almost all use majority voting. Only the cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel use proportional representation, and in Appenzell Innerrhoden the member of the Council of States is elected at the Landsgemeinde.

Most **cantonal governments** and many municipal councils are also elected by majority vote. Exceptions are, for example, the cantons of Ticino and Zug, which elect their government by proportional representation. The Federal Council is not elected by the people but by the United Federal Assembly. There, too, a person needs an absolute majority of the votes.

One advantage of majority voting is that well-known and popular personalities have a good chance. Those elected have the support of a broad majority. One disadvantage is that small parties hardly win any seats. The votes for the losers have no effect on the composition.

begriffe.erklaerung: One round of an election; sometimes two are needed.
More than half of the votes.
More votes than anyone else, even if it is less than half.
The small chamber of the federal parliament, which represents the cantons.

gewusst: Great Britain elects its House of Commons by majority vote; there, in each constituency, whoever has the most votes wins in the very first round.
In a majority election you can also write on the ballot paper the names of people who have not officially stood as candidates at all.

teile.einleitung: Lay judges help to reach verdicts in courts without having studied law. In Switzerland this is common above all in cantonal courts of first instance.
wichtigste: Lay judges have not completed any legal training.
They work mainly in lower courts such as the district courts.
The rules for this are made by the cantons, which is why they differ.
At the commercial and labour courts, expert judges from working life also take part in verdicts.
In the canton of Zurich the people elect the district judges.
Jury courts were abolished in 2011.

abschnitte.text: A **lay judge** has not completed a law degree. He or she brings **life experience** and knowledge from other professions into the court. In most cantons, lay judges take part in verdicts at criminal and civil courts of **first instance**, for example at the **district courts**. First instance means: this is where a case is judged for the first time. Because the cantons organise the courts themselves, the rules differ.

In the **canton of Zurich** the voters of a district elect their **district judges**. The fact that the people elect judges is a **Swiss peculiarity**. In **Aargau** any person **entitled to vote** can be elected as a justice of the peace, district judge or substitute judge. Legal training is not required for this.

At the **Zurich Commercial Court**, **commercial judges** from business sit alongside legally trained senior judges. They know companies and industries from their own experience. At the **labour court** there are expert judges from **employers'** and **employees'** circles. In this way practical knowledge from both sides goes into the verdict. Such a composition is called **parity-based**.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the jury courts
abschnitte.text: Some cantons used to have **jury courts**. There professional judges reached verdicts together with **jurors** from the general public. These courts were regarded as lengthy and expensive. They were abolished with the federal **Code of Criminal Procedure** of 2011. Lay judges are meant to bring an everyday view into the court and strengthen trust in the justice system. Critics doubt that this is still necessary today and would prefer only trained judges.

gewusst: The justice of the peace is often the first place to go in a dispute: he or she tries to get the parties to agree before it comes to a trial.
Since 2011 the same rules for criminal and civil proceedings have applied throughout Switzerland; before that each canton had its own.

teile.einleitung: The general strike (Landesstreik) of November 1918 was the largest general strike in the history of Switzerland. Around 250,000 workers downed tools to demand better living conditions and more political rights.
wichtigste: The general strike took place from 12 to 14 November 1918.
It began shortly after the end of the First World War.
The Olten Action Committee under Robert Grimm called the strike.
Around 250,000 people went on strike.
The first demand was a new election of the National Council by proportional representation.
In Grenchen three young workers died on the last day of the strike.

abschnitte.text: On **11 November 1918** the **First World War** ended with an armistice. Although Switzerland had not been involved in the war, many people suffered **hardship**. Food was scarce and expensive, and wages were often not enough. In addition, the **Spanish flu** was raging, and around 22,000 people in Switzerland died of it. The mood among workers was very tense.

The **Olten Action Committee**, made up of the Social Democratic Party and the trade unions, called for a strike. It was led by **Robert Grimm**. From 12 to 14 November 1918 around **250,000** people stopped work; that was a large part of the workforce. The Federal Council called up the **army** to keep order. After three days the committee called off the strike.

The strikers drew up a **nine-point programme**. First came the immediate **re-election of the National Council by proportional representation**. They also demanded the **48-hour week**, **votes for women** and old-age and disability insurance. Many demands were only met later: the National Council was first elected by proportional representation in 1919, the 48-hour week largely came in 1919 and 1920, and the AHV old-age insurance only in 1948.

On the last day of the strike, soldiers in **Grenchen** shot at strikers, and three young watch workers died. Around 1,500 soldiers who had been called up also died of the flu. After the strike Robert Grimm was sentenced to six months in prison. The general strike shaped the relationship between the middle classes and the workers for a long time. Today it is regarded as an important turning point in Swiss history.

gewusst: Votes for women, a demand from 1918, were only introduced at federal level in 1971.
Robert Grimm later became President of the National Council.

teile.einleitung: Lobbying means that interest groups try to influence politics. Associations, companies and organisations want to convince members of parliament of their concerns. In the Federal Palace this often happens in the lobby hall (Wandelhalle).
wichtigste: In lobbying, interest groups want to win members of parliament over to their concerns.
Each member of parliament may give two people a permanent access pass to the Federal Palace.
Anyone with such a permanent pass is listed in a public register.
Members of parliament must disclose their interests.
Informally this is called the godparent system.
The association Lobbywatch collects and publishes members' interests.
The lobby hall runs along the south side of the National Council chamber.

abschnitte.text: In **lobbying**, associations, companies or other organisations try to convince politicians of their concerns. This often happens in **personal conversations**. Lobbyists provide, for example, information or arguments about a law. Supporters say that this way members of parliament learn what a law means for those affected. Critics fear that groups with a lot of money and good connections gain too much influence.

You cannot simply walk into the **Federal Palace**. According to the **Parliament Act**, each member of parliament can give **two people** a permanent **access pass**. Many lobbyists gain access this way. Because they need a member of parliament as a “godfather” or “godmother” for this, it is called the **godparent system** (Götti-System). Critics complain that access thus depends on personal connections.

To make visible who is exerting influence, there are **public registers**. One shows who has a permanent pass, what role the person has and which member of parliament the pass comes from. In another register the members of parliament must state their **interests**, for example seats on company boards or work for associations. The association **Lobbywatch** also researches such connections and puts them online.

Many conversations take place in the **lobby hall**. It curves around the **south side** of the National Council chamber. The English word “lobby” originally means an entrance hall, which is where the term lobbying comes from. The lobby hall also serves as a **banqueting hall**, reception room and meeting place. Light materials such as **stucco** and **stucco marble** give it a friendly atmosphere.

The lobby hall is richly decorated. The **radiators** are clad in marble from Saillon in Valais, with **lions' heads** on them as decoration. The **ceiling paintings** were painted by the Ticino painter **Antonio Barzaghi-Cattaneo**. They are arranged in three rows. In the middle they show **six virtues** of the state.

gewusst: The word lobbying comes from the English “lobby”, which means entrance hall or lobby hall.
Even the radiators in the lobby hall of the Federal Palace are decorated with lions' heads.

teile.einleitung: The Laufen Valley (Laufental) is a German-speaking region on the River Birs. For a long time it belonged to the canton of Bern; since 1994 it has belonged to the canton of Basel-Landschaft. Getting there took almost twenty years and needed many votes.
wichtigste: The Laufen Valley is German-speaking, the canton of Jura is French-speaking.
The founding of the canton of Jura turned the Laufen Valley into a Bernese exclave.
In 1980 the Laufen Valley chose Basel-Landschaft as a possible partner canton.
In 1983 it first voted to stay with Bern, but the vote had to be repeated.
In 1989, 51.7 per cent said yes to moving to Basel-Landschaft.
In 1993 the people and the cantons of the whole of Switzerland agreed.
The district of Laufen has 13 municipalities.

abschnitte.text: Like the Jura, the Laufen Valley belonged to the canton of Bern for a long time. In the 1970s the people in the Jura voted on their future in several **plebiscites**. This led to the new **canton of Jura** in 1979. The German-speaking Laufen Valley did not want to join the French-speaking Jura. But because the new canton lay between the Laufen Valley and the rest of Bern, the valley became an **exclave**. This is an area that is cut off from the rest of its canton. The plebiscites gave the Laufen Valley the right to decide on a change.

In January 1980 the people of the Laufen Valley could choose between three cantons. **Basel-Landschaft** received 52 per cent, **Solothurn** 32 and **Basel-Stadt** 16 per cent. In March 1980 there followed a **run-off** between the two strongest. Basel-Landschaft won against Solothurn. This settled which canton would be negotiated with.

On **11 September 1983** the Laufen Valley voted. Just under 57 per cent wanted to stay with the canton of Bern. But in 1984 the **Bernese finance affair** came to light. The canton of Bern had secretly supported the pro-Bern campaign with money from secret funds. This is not allowed, because votes must be fair. The **Federal Supreme Court** therefore ordered the vote to be repeated.

On **12 November 1989** the Laufen Valley voted again. This time **51.7 per cent** said yes to the **Laufen Valley Treaty** and thus to joining Basel-Landschaft. Because this changed the borders of cantons, the whole of Switzerland also had to agree. On **26 September 1993** the **people and the cantons** said yes with around 75 per cent. Since 1 January 1994 the Laufen Valley has belonged to Basel-Landschaft.

Today the Laufen Valley forms the **district of Laufen**. It is one of five districts of the canton of Basel-Landschaft and has **13 municipalities**. They include, for example, Laufen, Zwingen, Grellingen and Röschenz. The **Birs** flows through the valley. The history of the Laufen Valley shows how border questions, too, are solved democratically in Switzerland.

gewusst: Before the final move, the Laufen Valley voted several times, and in the end even the whole of Switzerland had a say.
Because Bern put money into the campaign without permission in 1983, the result of the vote was declared invalid.

teile.einleitung: The left-right scheme is a simple way of ordering parties and political opinions. You imagine a line: on the left are parties that want more equality through the state, on the right those that emphasise more freedom for the economy and the individual.
wichtigste: The terms left and right come from France.
They arose in 1789 from the seating arrangement in the French National Assembly.
Left-wing parties usually call for more redistribution by the state.
Parties to the right of centre usually want lower taxes and less state.
Among the Federal Council parties, the SP is furthest to the left and the SVP furthest to the right.
The SVP, FDP and the Centre are often called the bourgeois parties.
A second axis distinguishes between liberal and conservative.

abschnitte.text: The division into left and right comes from **France**. In **1789**, at the time of the French Revolution, the **National Assembly** was meeting. Seen from the president, the supporters of great changes sat on the **left** side. The supporters of the king and the old order sat on the **right**. Over time this **seating arrangement** gave rise to political terms that are still used all over the world today.

**Left-wing** parties want to reduce the differences between rich and poor. They support a strong **welfare state** and want more **redistribution**. This means: the state takes in money through taxes and spends it, for example, on social benefits, education or health. In Switzerland the **SP** and the **Greens** in particular count as left-wing parties.

Parties **to the right of centre** want the state to hold back. They often call for **lower taxes** and fewer regulations, so that the economy can act as freely as possible. Many also emphasise personal responsibility and tradition. The **SVP** represents national-conservative positions and is furthest to the right among the Federal Council parties. **The SVP, FDP and the Centre** are together often referred to as the **bourgeois parties**, in contrast to the SP and the Greens.

Between left and right lies the **centre**. Centre parties take more left-wing positions on some topics and more right-wing ones on others. One example is the **Green Liberals (GLP)**. On environmental questions they are close to the Greens, on economic questions close to the FDP. That is why they are usually placed in the centre.

A single line is often not enough to describe parties precisely. A party can, for example, be economically right-wing but socially open. That is why people often draw a **second axis** between **liberal** and **conservative**. Liberal here means open to new things and to many ways of life; conservative means rather holding on to what has proved itself. This creates a field with four corners into which you can place parties and also your own opinions.

gewusst: The terms left and right are over 230 years old and go back to a simple seating arrangement.
Online voting aids show voters where they themselves stand in the political field.

teile.einleitung: The Landsgemeinde of Appenzell Innerrhoden is an open-air assembly at which the voters vote and elect. It takes place every year in the village of Appenzell and is one of the oldest forms of democracy.
wichtigste: The Landsgemeinde takes place in the cantonal capital Appenzell.
It is normally held on the last Sunday in April.
Only Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden still have a Landsgemeinde.
Appenzell Ausserrhoden abolished its Landsgemeinde in 1997.
Women in Innerrhoden have only been able to vote since 1991.
The Landsgemeinde also elects the government and the court.

abschnitte.text: The Innerrhoden **Landsgemeinde** is normally held on the **last Sunday in April**. If this day falls on **Easter**, it is held a week later, on the first Sunday in May. The meeting place is the **Landsgemeinde square** in the cantonal capital **Appenzell**. The voters stand together there in the **ring**.

In the morning the government and many people attend a **church service**. Afterwards a ceremonial **procession** moves from the **town hall** to the Landsgemeinde square. The government walks in it too. Many men traditionally carry a sword or a side arm, which used to count as proof of the right to vote. For many people of Innerrhoden the Landsgemeinde is a day of celebration.

At the Landsgemeinde voting is done **openly**: anyone who agrees raises their hand. This is called a **show of hands**. The voters decide on laws and elect the government, which in Innerrhoden is called the **Standeskommission**. The **court** is also elected at the Landsgemeinde. Everything happens in the open air.

Appenzell Innerrhoden was the **last canton** to introduce votes for women at cantonal level. The men had rejected it several times at the Landsgemeinde. In November 1990 the **Federal Supreme Court** decided that women in Innerrhoden must also be allowed to vote. In **April 1991** women stood in the ring for the first time.

In the past several cantons had a Landsgemeinde. Today it only exists in **Glarus** and **Appenzell Innerrhoden**. **Appenzell Ausserrhoden** voted at the ballot box in **1997** to abolish it. Since then votes there are only held at the ballot box. Supporters value the tradition and the sense of community at the Landsgemeinde; critics complain that the vote is not secret.

gewusst: At federal level women in Switzerland have been able to vote since 1971; in Innerrhoden at cantonal level only 20 years later.
Appenzell Innerrhoden is one of the smallest cantons in Switzerland, which is why almost all the voters fit into the Landsgemeinde square.

teile.einleitung: The Lega dei Ticinesi is a political party in the canton of Ticino. It was founded in 1991 as a protest party and today is represented in the Ticino government and in the National Council.
wichtigste: The Lega dei Ticinesi was founded in January 1991.
Its founders were the businessman Giuliano Bignasca and the journalist Flavio Maspoli.
The party publishes the free Sunday newspaper “Il Mattino della domenica”.
Since 2011 it has provided two of the five members of the Ticino Council of State.
In the Federal Palace its representatives belong to the SVP parliamentary group.
Important topics are cross-border commuters and criticism of the EU.

abschnitte.text: The **Lega dei Ticinesi** was founded in January 1991. Behind it were the businessman **Giuliano Bignasca** and the journalist **Flavio Maspoli**. They wanted to protest against the established parties and against the authorities in “Bern”. In its very first year the Lega won a seat in the **National Council**. Giuliano Bignasca was president of the party for a long time; he died in 2013.

The Lega publishes the **“Mattino della domenica”**. This is a free newspaper that appears on Sundays. It is regarded as the mouthpiece of the party. The newspaper is known for its **provocative style** with sharp headlines. Supporters value the direct language; critics often find it hurtful.

The Lega has been represented in the Ticino **Council of State**, the cantonal government, since 1995. Since 2011 it has provided **two of the five** members. A well-known Lega politician was **Marco Borradori**. He was a member of the Council of State for a long time and mayor of **Lugano** from 2013 to 2021. He was regarded as the moderate face of the party and died in office in 2021.

Since the 2023 elections the Lega has held one of Ticino's eight seats in the National Council. It is held by **Lorenzo Quadri**, who has sat in the National Council since 2011. With so few seats the Lega cannot form its own **parliamentary group**. Its representatives therefore join the **SVP group**. In 2015 the Ticino councillor of state **Norman Gobbi** of the Lega was on the SVP's official ticket of three candidates for the Federal Council. Guy Parmelin was elected at the time.

One main topic of the Lega is **cross-border commuters**. These are people from Italy who work in Ticino and commute across the border every day. The Lega criticises that they compete with Ticino workers. The party also rejects **joining the EU** and criticises the federal authorities. Other parties counter that the Ticino economy depends on cross-border commuters.

gewusst: The Lega made it into the National Council in the very year it was founded.
The name “Lega dei Ticinesi” means “League of Ticinese” in English.

teile.einleitung: A consultative vote is a non-binding poll of the people on a particular question. The authorities want to find out what the population thinks, but they do not have to stick to the result. This makes it very different from the normal popular votes in Switzerland.
wichtigste: A consultative vote is a non-binding poll of the people.
The result is not legally binding.
Consultative means advisory.
The normal popular votes in Switzerland, by contrast, are binding.
At federal level Switzerland does not provide for consultative votes.
Politically, the result of such a poll often carries great weight all the same.

abschnitte.text: The word **consultative** comes from the Latin consultare and means advisory or asking for advice. In a consultative vote the people vote on a question, just as in a real vote. But the result is only a **recommendation** to the government or parliament. In the end the authorities may also decide differently.

In Switzerland popular votes are normally **binding**. If the people accept an initiative, it becomes part of the constitution, and if they reject a law, it does not come into force. With a consultative vote this is not the case. That is why there are none at federal level in Switzerland; there the people always decide in a binding way.

Some cantons and municipalities nevertheless have non-binding **public consultations**. A municipality can, for example, ask the population whether they could imagine a merger with the neighbouring village. The result helps the authorities to plan the next steps. Each canton decides for itself whether such polls are allowed.

In many countries public polls are rare and often only advisory. In Austria a non-binding **public poll** on compulsory military service took place in January 2013, and the majority voted to keep it. The 2016 vote on Great Britain leaving the EU was also legally only advisory. The government nevertheless carried out the result, **Brexit**, because it wanted to respect the will of the majority.

One advantage is that the authorities learn the opinion of the population before they decide. Critics say such polls could disappoint people if the authorities do not carry out the result in the end. In addition, it is often unclear how much a narrow result should count. That is why consultative votes are controversial in Switzerland and rather the **exception**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Advisory, meant only as a recommendation.
Must be complied with.
A vote used to find out the opinion of the population.
The joining of two or more municipalities into one.

gewusst: Brexit was carried out on the basis of a vote that was legally only advisory.
In Switzerland the people always have the last word in votes at federal level; a mere poll does not exist there.

teile.einleitung: Consociational democracy (in German “Konkordanzdemokratie”) is a form of democracy in which as many of the important forces as possible govern together. In Switzerland this means: the largest parties sit together in the Federal Council, instead of a majority governing and the others going into opposition. The word concordance comes from Latin and means agreement.
wichtigste: In a consociational democracy the largest parties govern together.
That is why Switzerland has no strong opposition as other countries do.
Solutions are found through negotiations and compromises.
From 1959 to 2003 the so-called magic formula applied in the Federal Council.
The opposite is competitive democracy with a government and an opposition.
Popular rights such as the referendum have strongly encouraged concordance.

abschnitte.text: In a **consociational democracy** as many parties and groups as possible should share in power. Instead of the majority deciding alone, people look for solutions that many can live with. This is also called a **compromise**. In Switzerland this can be seen above all in the composition of the Federal Council.

In countries such as Germany or Great Britain there is a **competitive democracy**. There the party or coalition with the majority forms the government. The other parties are in **opposition** and criticise the government. After elections the government can change completely, which hardly ever happens in Switzerland.

After the federal state was founded in 1848, at first only the Liberals (Freisinnige) provided all the federal councillors. In 1891 Josef Zemp became the first Catholic Conservative to be elected, and in 1943 Ernst Nobs the first Social Democrat. In 1959 the **magic formula** came into being: two seats for the FDP, two for the CVP, two for the SP and one for the SVP. This distribution remained unchanged until 2003.

In 2003 the SVP, as the strongest party, received a second seat, and the CVP lost one in return. Today the SVP, SP and FDP each have two seats and the Centre (Die Mitte) has one. The parties try to reflect their strength in elections roughly in the Federal Council. However, there are repeated arguments about what a fair distribution is.

An important reason is **popular rights**. With a referendum, groups that were not allowed to have a say can bring down a law at the ballot box. That is why it pays to involve all important forces early on, for example in the **consultation procedure**, in which parties and associations give their opinion on new laws. The variety of languages, religions and regions has also helped Switzerland to rely on balance.

Concordance ensures **stability**, because politics does not change greatly after every election. Many people feel represented because their party is part of the government. Critics say that decisions therefore take a long time and responsibilities are less clear. In addition, there is no clear opposition to keep a check on the government; this role is often taken on by the people and the media.

begriffe.erklaerung: Agreement; here: many parties governing together.
Parties that are not in the government and criticise it.
The fixed distribution of Federal Council seats from 1959 to 2003.
A solution in which all sides give way a little.
Asking parties, cantons and associations for their views on a new law.

gewusst: The magic formula stayed the same for 44 years, from 1959 to 2003.
In Switzerland there is no change of government after elections as in many other countries.
In many cantons and municipalities, too, several parties sit together in the government.

teile.einleitung: A majority means that more than half have decided the same way. In a democracy this is how it is settled which proposal is accepted or who is elected. But there are different kinds of majority, and in Switzerland sometimes two are even needed at the same time.
wichtigste: Majority means that more than half have decided the same way.
With a simple majority, one side has more votes than the other.
An absolute majority requires more than half of all valid votes.
Some decisions need a qualified majority, for example two thirds.
Changes to the constitution in Switzerland need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
There are 23 cantonal votes because six cantons only have half a vote.
In a democracy the rights of the minority must also be protected.

abschnitte.text: A **majority** is the larger part of a group. If, in a class of 24 children, 13 vote for a trip to the zoo, that is a majority. The other 11 children form the **minority**. In a democracy, what the majority has decided usually applies.

With a **simple majority**, the proposal with more yes than no votes wins. With an absolute majority you need more than half of all valid votes, that is more than all the others put together. With a **qualified majority** even more is needed, for example two thirds. Such strict rules often apply to particularly important decisions, for example changes to the rules of a club.

abschnitte.titel: Majority of the people and of the cantons
abschnitte.text: In a federal vote on a change to the constitution, two majorities are needed. The **majority of the people** means that more than half of those voting in the whole of Switzerland say yes. The **majority of the cantons** means that yes is also said in the majority of the cantons. For simple referendums on laws, on the other hand, the majority of the people is enough.

Switzerland has 26 cantons but only 23 **cantonal votes**. The six former half-cantons Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each have half a vote. For a majority of the cantons you need at least twelve cantonal votes. In a tie of 11.5 to 11.5, the proposal is rejected.

The majority may not decide everything. The **fundamental rights** in the Federal Constitution protect all people, even if they are in the minority. Switzerland also makes sure that language groups and small cantons can have a say. That is why, for example, there is the Council of States, in which every canton has the same number of seats, no matter how big it is.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smaller part of a group in a vote.
The majority of all voters in the whole of Switzerland.
The majority of the cantons in a vote.
A particularly large majority, for example two thirds.

gewusst: It has happened that a proposal had a majority of the people but failed to win a majority of the cantons, for example the Responsible Business Initiative in 2020.
Blank ballot papers are not counted in federal votes when the result is calculated.

teile.einleitung: A letter to the editor is a text in which readers of a newspaper give their opinion. This allows everyone to join in public discussion, not just journalists.
wichtigste: A letter to the editor is one of the opinion-based types of text.
Letters to the editor often appear in a section called “Forum” or “Letters”.
The editors may shorten letters, but must not change their meaning.
Insults are not printed, because the newspaper shares responsibility.
Before votes there is often a deadline for submissions.
Online, the reader comment under the article is the counterpart.

abschnitte.titel: What a letter to the editor is
abschnitte.text: In a **letter to the editor**, someone from the public reacts to an article or to a current topic. It expresses a personal opinion. That is why, like the commentary, it is one of the **opinion-based types of text**. The difference: a **commentary** is written by someone on the editorial staff, a letter to the editor by someone from the public. Many newspapers collect the letters on a page of their own, often called **“Forum”**.

Not every letter to the editor is printed. The editors choose and may **shorten** letters if they are too long. However, the **meaning** must be kept. A newspaper does not print letters containing **insults**. Anyone who publishes an insult can share the blame, even if it comes from someone else. Writers usually have to give their name and where they live.

abschnitte.titel: Letters to the editor before votes
abschnitte.text: Before votes and elections newspapers receive especially many letters. Many editorial teams therefore set a **deadline for submissions**. A few days before voting day, no new letters on the topic appear. This leaves time to respond to claims. Sometimes an organisation has many similar letters sent in by different people. This is called a **letter-writing campaign**. It is meant to give the impression that an opinion is widespread.

On news websites there is the **reader comment**. There readers write their opinion directly under an article. This is quicker than a letter, and others often reply straight away. These comments are also often checked by the editors before or after they appear. The rules are similar: stay factual and do not insult anyone.

abschnitte.titel: Tips for a good letter to the editor
abschnitte.text: A good letter to the editor is **short** and sticks to one topic. It says which article it refers to. Your own opinion is backed up with **reasons** so that others understand it. You criticise ideas, not people. In this way a letter to the editor contributes to a fair discussion in a democracy.

gewusst: A letter to the editor can also contain praise, not just criticism.
Politicians also write letters to the editor to promote their views.

teile.einleitung: The Mass Immigration Initiative was a popular initiative of the SVP. On 9 February 2014 the people and the cantons accepted it by a very narrow margin. It demanded that Switzerland control immigration itself, and it greatly changed relations with the EU.
wichtigste: The initiative “Against mass immigration” was launched by the SVP.
It was accepted on 9 February 2014 with 50.3 per cent voting yes.
The difference was only around 19,300 votes.
It demanded maximum numbers and quotas for immigration.
This brought it into conflict with the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons with the EU.
Article 121a was newly added to the Federal Constitution.
Parliament implemented it in December 2016 with the “light” priority for domestic workers.

abschnitte.text: The **SVP** launched the popular initiative **“Against mass immigration”**. It wanted Switzerland to control immigration itself again. On **9 February 2014** the people voted. **50.3 per cent** said yes. There were 1,463,854 yes votes and 1,444,552 no votes, so the difference was only **19,302 votes**. It was one of the narrowest results of recent decades.

The initiative added **Article 121a** to the Federal Constitution. It is in the section on foreign nationals. Every year **maximum numbers** and **quotas** for foreign nationals were to be set. In doing so, the interests of the economy were to be taken into account. A **transitional provision** required that conflicting treaties be renegotiated within **three years**.

Switzerland has the **Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons** with the EU. It allows EU citizens to live and work in Switzerland, and vice versa. **Quotas** contradict this principle.
